DNA: Uncovering Universal Latent Forgery Knowledge

Look for forgery-sensitive anchors already encoded in pretrained models instead of relying only on end-to-end adaptation.

Dou Jingtong

January 30, 2026 ·ICML 2026 ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

DNA searches a frozen visual backbone for forgery-discriminative units through a coarse-to-fine procedure. Layer-level geometry narrows the search, while a triadic score and curvature-based selection identify sparse units. A lightweight detector then uses those units to distinguish authentic and synthetic images.

The HIFI-Gen evaluation examines transfer to generators and architectures outside training. This places the emphasis on whether selected representations carry reusable forensic information, beyond the signatures of the generators used to build the detector.

FDUsForgery-discriminative units
Few-shotLimited-supervision detection
HIFI-GenHigh-fidelity generation benchmark

Generalizable forgery detection can begin with discriminative structure already present in pretrained features.

Why this matters

Task-level adaptation can conceal which pretrained components already carry forensic information. The study asks whether a compact set of such components can serve as a detection basis.

How it works

  1. Analyze feature decoupling and attention shifts to locate critical intermediate layers.
  2. Combine triadic scoring with curvature truncation to select forgery-discriminative units.
  3. Evaluate selected anchors on forgery benchmarks, including the introduced HIFI-Gen dataset.

What the study finds

The paper reports strong few-shot detection and robustness across evaluated architectures and unseen generators. Its experiments examine the usefulness of the selected anchors under distribution changes.

What this means

The key question in forensics is what survives the next change in generation technology. Internal localization offers a way to investigate that question at the representation level, by examining which discriminative coordinates remain informative when the source of synthetic images changes.

The work suggests a path from pretrained knowledge to a compact, inspectable detection interface. Generalization remains an empirical claim tied to the tested shifts; broader deployment calls for continued evaluation on new generators, processing pipelines, and authentic-image distributions.
